mishnayos.summary: Almost anyone may shecht an animal, and the shechitah is kosher. A non-Jew's shechitah makes the animal a neveilah, but shechting at night, by a blind person, or even on Shabbos, is still kosher.

chunks.en: Everyone may shecht, and their shechitah is kosher,
chunks.st: Everyone slaughters an animal, i.e., can perform halakhically valid slaughter, and their slaughter is valid,

words.note: Shechitah is the kosher way of slaughtering an animal.

chunks.en: except for a deaf-mute,
chunks.st: except for a deaf-mute,

words.note: Someone who cannot hear or speak; the halachah treats him as not responsible.

chunks.en: someone who is not mentally fit, and a child,
chunks.st: an imbecile, and a minor,

chunks.en: because they might ruin their shechitah.
chunks.st: lest they ruin their slaughter because they lack competence.

chunks.en: But if any of them shechted and others watched them,
chunks.st: And for all of them, when they slaughtered an animal and others see and supervise

chunks.en: their shechitah is kosher.
chunks.st: them, their slaughter is valid.

chunks.en: The shechitah of a non-Jew
chunks.st: Slaughter performed by a gentile renders the animal

chunks.en: makes it a neveilah, and it makes a person tamei by carrying it.
chunks.st: an unslaughtered carcass, and the carcass imparts ritual impurity through carrying.

words.note: An animal that died without a kosher shechitah.

chunks.en: Someone who shechts at night,
chunks.st: In the case of one who slaughters an animal at night,

chunks.st: his slaughter is valid.

chunks.en: Someone who shechts on Shabbos
chunks.st: In the case of one who slaughters an animal on Shabbat

chunks.st: or on Yom Kippur,

chunks.en: even though he deserves the death penalty for it,
chunks.st: although he is liable to receive the death penalty,

chunks.en: his shechitah is kosher.
chunks.st: his slaughter is valid.

mishnayos.summary: You may shecht with a smooth sickle, a sharp stone or a reed. You may not shecht with a saw, teeth or a fingernail, because they choke the animal instead of cutting.

chunks.en: Someone who shechts with a hand sickle,

chunks.st: In the case of one who slaughters an animal with the smooth side of a hand sickle, which has both a smooth and a serrated side,

chunks.en: with a sharp stone, or with a reed,
chunks.st: or with a sharpened flint, or with a reed that was cut lengthwise and sharpened,

chunks.en: his shechitah is kosher.
chunks.st: his slaughter is valid.

chunks.en: Anyone may shecht, and at any time one may shecht,
chunks.st: All slaughter [hakkol shoḥatin], and one may always slaughter,

chunks.en: and one may shecht with anything,
chunks.st: and one may slaughter with any item that cuts,

chunks.en: except for a harvest sickle,
chunks.explain: It has teeth, like a saw.
chunks.st: except for the serrated side of the harvest sickle,

chunks.en: a saw, and teeth,
chunks.st: a saw, the teeth of an animal when attached to its jawbone,

chunks.en: and a fingernail, because they choke the animal.
chunks.st: and a fingernail, because they are serrated and they consequently strangle the animal and do not cut its windpipe and gullet as required.

chunks.en: Someone who shechts with a harvest sickle, moving it forward,
chunks.st: In the case of one who slaughters an animal with a harvest sickle, which is serrated with its teeth inclined considerably in one direction, in a forward direction, where the serrations do not tear the flesh,

chunks.en: Beis Shammai say it is pasul,
chunks.st: Beit Shammai deem the slaughter not valid

chunks.en: and Beis Hillel say it is kosher.
chunks.st: and Beit Hillel deem it valid.

chunks.en: And if its teeth were smoothed down,
chunks.st: And they both agree that if they smoothed its serrations so that they do not tear the flesh, its halakhic status

chunks.en: it is just like a knife.
chunks.st: is like that of a knife and one may slaughter with it.

mishnayos.summary: The shechitah cut belongs below the ring at the top of the windpipe. If he cut inside the ring but left a thin line of it whole, it is still kosher.

chunks.en: Someone who shechts inside the ring and left of it
chunks.explain: The ring is the hard ring at the top of the windpipe.
chunks.st: With regard to one who slaughters an animal from within the cricoid cartilage that forms a complete ring at the top of the windpipe

chunks.en: a thread's width all around it,
chunks.st: and left a thread breadth over the surface of the ring in its entirety intact, as the knife did not go beyond the ring toward the head of the animal,

chunks.en: his shechitah is kosher.
chunks.st: his slaughter is valid.

chunks.en: Rabbi Yosei the son of Yehudah says:

mishnayos.summary: Shechitah is done from the front of the neck, but melikah (the way a Kohen kills a bird korban with his fingernail) is done from the back of the neck. What is right for one is wrong for the other.

chunks.en: Someone who shechts from the sides, his shechitah is kosher.
chunks.st: One who slaughters from the sides of the throat, his slaughter is valid.

chunks.en: Someone who does melikah from the sides,
chunks.explain: Melikah: the Kohen cuts a bird korban's neck with his fingernail.
chunks.st: One who pinches the neck of a bird offering from the sides,

chunks.en: his melikah is pasul.
chunks.st: his pinching is not valid.

chunks.en: Someone who shechts from the back of the neck,
chunks.st: One who slaughters from the nape [oref] of the neck,

chunks.en: his shechitah is pasul.
chunks.st: his slaughter is not valid.

chunks.en: Someone who does melikah from the back of the neck,
chunks.st: One who pinches a bird offering from the nape of the neck,

chunks.en: his melikah is kosher.
chunks.st: his pinching is valid.

chunks.en: Someone who shechts from the front of the neck,
chunks.st: One who slaughters from the throat,

chunks.en: his shechitah is kosher.
chunks.st: his slaughter is valid.

chunks.en: Someone who does melikah from the front of the neck,
chunks.st: One who pinches a bird offering from the throat,

chunks.en: his melikah is pasul,
chunks.st: his pinching is not valid,

chunks.en: because the whole back of the neck is right for melikah,
chunks.st: as the entire nape is valid for pinching

chunks.en: and the whole front of the neck is right for shechitah.
chunks.st: and the entire throat is valid for slaughter.

chunks.en: So we find: what is kosher for shechitah
chunks.st: It is found that that which is valid for slaughter is

chunks.en: is pasul for melikah,
chunks.st: not

chunks.en: and what is kosher for melikah
chunks.st: valid for pinching and that which is valid for pinching is

chunks.en: is pasul for shechitah.
chunks.st: not valid for slaughter.

chunks.st: is unfit for sacrifice in doves.

chunks.en: When the feathers start to turn yellow,

mishnayos.summary: The mishnah lists more pairs where something that is right in one case is wrong in another: two kinds of special cows, Kohanim and Levi'im, different kinds of vessels, and bitter and sweet almonds.

chunks.st: That which is fit in a red heifer

mishnayos.summary: More pairs: temed (a weak drink made from grape leftovers), brothers who are partners, a girl's father, yibum, and Yom Tov next to Shabbos. Where one rule applies, the other does not.

chunks.en: Temed, before it turned sour,
chunks.explain: Temed is water soaked in leftover grape skins.

chunks.en: may not be bought with ma'aser money,
chunks.explain: Ma'aser sheni money is spent on food in Yerushalayim.

chunks.en: and it makes a mikveh pasul.
Once it fermented, it may be bought with ma'aser money, and it does not
make a mikveh pasul.
Brothers who are partners,
when they must add the kalbon,
chunks.explain: A small extra coin added to the half-shekel.

chunks.en: do not need to give ma'aser from their animals.
When they must give ma'aser from their animals,
they do not need to add the kalbon.
Whenever a father may sell his daughter as a maidservant,

chunks.en: And whenever there is a fine,
there is no selling.

"He who separates between holy and holy."

mishnayos.summary: For a kosher shechitah, a bird needs one of its two simanim (the windpipe and the food pipe) cut, and an animal needs both. Cutting most of a siman counts like cutting all of it.

chunks.en: Someone who shechts one siman in a bird,
chunks.explain: The simanim are the windpipe and the food pipe.
chunks.st: In the case of one who slaughters by cutting one siman, i.e., the windpipe or the gullet, in a bird,

chunks.en: and two simanim in an animal,
chunks.st: and two simanim in an animal,

chunks.st: his slaughter is valid,

chunks.st: Rabbi Yehuda says: The slaughter is not valid

chunks.en: his shechitah is kosher.
chunks.st: his slaughter is valid.

mishnayos.summary: Shechting two animals at the same time is kosher. Two people may also hold a knife (or two knives) and shecht one animal together.

chunks.en: Someone who shechts two heads at the same time,
chunks.st: With regard to one who slaughters by cutting two animals’ heads simultaneously,

chunks.en: his shechitah is kosher.
chunks.st: his slaughter is valid.

mishnayos.summary: The knife must move back and forth; chopping off the head in one blow is pasul unless the knife is very long. A knife that fell and cut by itself is pasul, and stopping in the middle of shechitah for too long makes it pasul.

chunks.en: If he cut off the head in one blow,
chunks.st: If one decapitated the animal in one motion and did not slaughter the animal in the standard manner of drawing the knife back and forth,

chunks.en: it is pasul.
chunks.st: the slaughter is not valid.

chunks.en: If he was shechting and cut off the head in one blow,

chunks.en: And with grasshoppers: any that has four legs,
chunks.st: And with regard to grasshoppers, whose signs were also not stated in the Torah, the Sages stated: Any grasshopper that has four legs,

chunks.en: and four wings,
chunks.st: and four wings,

chunks.en: and jumping legs, and its wings cover most of it.
chunks.st: and two additional jumping legs, and whose wings cover most of its body, is kosher.

chunks.he: וּבַדָּגִים, כֹּל שֶׁיֶּשׁ לוֹ סְנַפִּיר וְקַשְׂקָשֶׂת.

chunks.en: And fins are what it swims with.
chunks.st: and fins are those with which the fish swims.

chunks.st: Even if an animal was encountering difficulty giving birth and meanwhile

chunks.st: the fetus extended its foreleg outside the mother animal’s womb and then brought it back inside,

chunks.en: may be eaten.
chunks.explain: When the mother is shechted, the calf is allowed with her.
chunks.st: and then the mother animal was slaughtered, the consumption of the fetus is permitted
chunks.stMore: by virtue of the slaughter of the mother animal.

chunks.en: If it put out its head,
chunks.st: But if the fetus extended its head outside the womb,

chunks.en: even though it pulled it back,
chunks.st: even if it then brought it back inside, the halakhic status of

chunks.st: that fetus is like that of a newborn,

chunks.en: If he cuts pieces off the unborn calf inside her,

chunks.en: But pieces from the spleen and from the kidneys

chunks.en: may not be eaten.

chunks.en: This is the rule:
chunks.st: This is the principle:

mishnayos.stIntro: When a pregnant kosher animal is slaughtered, the slaughter also renders the consumption of its fetus permitted.

mishnayos.summary: A baby bechor (firstborn animal) is holy once it is born. If the mother had trouble giving birth and he had to cut up the calf before it was born, it is not holy; if most of it came out, it must be buried.

chunks.en: An animal having her first calf, with a hard birth:
chunks.st: If an animal that was giving birth to a firstborn male was encountering difficulty giving birth, and in order to alleviate the difficulty one wishes to terminate the birth,

chunks.en: he may cut it up piece by piece and throw it to the dogs.
chunks.explain: Because it was not born yet, it is not holy.
chunks.st: he may cut up the fetus limb by limb and cast it to the dogs. Since the fetus was not born, it is non-sacred and does not require burial.

chunks.en: If most of it came out,
chunks.st: If a majority of the fetus had already emerged, it is considered to have been born and is therefore consecrated; consequently, if one cut it up

chunks.en: it must be buried,
chunks.st: it must be buried, and the mother animal is

chunks.en: and the mother is free from the bechor rule.
chunks.explain: Her later calves will not be holy as a bechor.
chunks.st: exempted from having firstborn status conferred on any future offspring.

mishnayos.stIntro: Upon its birth, the firstborn male offspring of a domesticated animal is automatically consecrated with firstborn status, and it is prohibited to derive benefit from it. Furthermore, if it dies, it may not be discarded, but must be buried.

mishnayos.summary: If an unborn animal died inside its mother and the shepherd touched it, he stays tahor. But if a woman's unborn baby died and the midwife touched it, the midwife becomes tamei for seven days.

chunks.he: בְּהֵמָה שֶׁמֵּת עֻבָּרָהּ בְּתוֹךְ מֵעֶיהָ וְהוֹשִׁיט
chunks.en: An animal whose unborn calf died inside her, and the shepherd reached in
his hand and touched it,
whether in a non-kosher animal,
or in a kosher animal,
he is tahor. Rabbi Yosei HaGelili says:
In a non-kosher animal, he is tamei,
and in a kosher animal, he is tahor.

chunks.he: הָאִשָּׁה שֶׁמֵּת וְלָדָהּ בְּתוֹךְ מֵעֶיהָ וּפָשְׁטָה
chunks.en: A woman whose unborn baby died inside her, and the midwife
reached in her hand and touched it:
the midwife becomes tamei for seven days,
and the woman stays tahor until the baby comes out.

mishnayos.summary: If an unborn calf's leg came out and was cut off after the mother was shechted, Rabbi Meir says the meat touched a neveilah, and the Sages disagree. The mishnah then shows how we know that shechting a treifah keeps it from being a tamei neveilah.

chunks.en: An animal having a hard time giving birth,
chunks.st: If an animal was encountering difficulty giving birth

chunks.en: and the unborn calf put out its front leg, and he cut it off,
chunks.st: and as a result the fetus extended its foreleg outside the mother’s womb, and someone severed it

chunks.en: and afterwards he shechted its mother:
chunks.st: and afterward slaughtered the mother animal,

chunks.en: the meat is tahor.
chunks.st: the flesh of the fetus is ritually pure.

chunks.he: שָׁחַט אֶת אִמּוֹ וְאַחַר כָּךְ חֲתָכָהּ,
chunks.en: If he shechted its mother and afterwards cut off the leg,
chunks.st: If one first slaughtered the mother animal and afterward severed the foreleg,

chunks.en: the meat has touched a neveilah.
chunks.explain: The cut-off leg counts as a neveilah.
chunks.st: the flesh of both the mother animal and the fetus are ritually impure due to having been in contact with a carcass.
chunks.stMore: Since the foreleg was not permitted to be consumed through the act of slaughtering, it is regarded as a carcass with the associated ritual impurity. The rest of the flesh, which was permitted to be consumed by the slaughter, was in contact with it and so was rendered ritually impure from it;

chunks.en: That is what Rabbi Meir says.
chunks.st: this is the statement of Rabbi Meir.

chunks.en: And the Sages say:
chunks.st: And the Rabbis say: The flesh has the ritual impurity of having been in

chunks.en: It touched a treifah that was shechted.
chunks.explain: That is a lighter kind of tumah.
chunks.st: contact with a tereifa that was slaughtered,
chunks.stMore: as the limb is regarded as a tereifa that was slaughtered. By Torah law, although it is prohibited to consume it, it does not impart ritual impurity. Nevertheless, the Sages decreed that a tereifa that was slaughtered, as well as anything that comes in contact with it, is regarded as ritually impure to the extent that it disqualifies sacrificial foods that come in contact with it.

chunks.en: Just as we find that a treifah's shechitah makes it tahor,
chunks.st: The Rabbis explain the rationale behind their opinion: Just as we found in the case of a tereifa that its slaughter renders it ritually pure according to Torah law,
chunks.stMore: i.e., ritual slaughter prevents it from having the ritual impurity of a carcass despite not rendering the animal permitted for consumption,

chunks.he: אַף שְׁחִיטַת בְּהֵמָה תְּטַהֵר אֶת הָאֵבָר.
chunks.en: so too the shechitah of the mother should make the leg tahor.
chunks.st: so too, the slaughter of the mother animal should render the limb of its fetus that left the womb ritually pure,
chunks.stMore: despite the fact that its consumption is prohibited.

chunks.en: Rabbi Meir said to them:
chunks.st: Rabbi Meir said to them:

chunks.he: לֹא, אִם טִהֲרָה שְׁחִיטַת טְרֵפָה אוֹתָהּ,
chunks.en: No! If a treifah's shechitah makes it tahor,
chunks.st: No, if the slaughter of a tereifa renders the body of the animal ritually pure,

chunks.en: that is something that is part of its body.
chunks.st: it is because the slaughter is performed on something that is part of its body, i.e., its throat.

chunks.en: Should it make the leg tahor,
chunks.st: Does it necessarily follow that you should also render the limb that left the womb pure,

chunks.en: something that is not part of its body?
chunks.st: given that it is something that is not part of the mother’s body? Certainly not.

chunks.en: How do we know that a treifah's shechitah makes it tahor?
chunks.st: The mishna asks: From where is it derived with regard to a tereifa that its slaughter renders it ritually pure, i.e., prevents it from having the ritual impurity of a carcass?
chunks.stMore: The mishna notes there is a reason to say the slaughter should not render it pure, as one can compare a tereifa with a non-kosher animal:

chunks.en: A non-kosher animal may not be eaten,
chunks.st: A non-kosher animal is prohibited for consumption;

chunks.en: and a treifah may not be eaten.
chunks.st: so too, a tereifa is prohibited for consumption.

chunks.he: מַה בְּהֵמָה טְמֵאָה אֵין שְׁחִיטָתָהּ מְטַהַרְתָּהּ,
chunks.en: Just as a non-kosher animal's shechitah does not make it tahor,
chunks.st: Therefore, conclude: Just as with regard to a non-kosher animal, its slaughter does not render it ritually pure,

chunks.en: so too a treifah's shechitah should not make it tahor!
chunks.st: so too with regard to a tereifa, its slaughter should not render it ritually pure.

chunks.he: לֹא, אִם אָמַרְתָּ בִּבְהֵמָה טְמֵאָה שֶׁלֹּא
chunks.en: No! If you said this about a non-kosher animal, which never
chunks.st: The mishna questions the comparison: No, if you said that slaughtering cannot prevent an animal from having the ritual impurity of a carcass in the case of a non-kosher animal,

chunks.en: had a time when it could be kosher,
chunks.st: which is distinct in that it did not have a period of potential fitness
chunks.stMore: when slaughtering it could have rendered its consumption permitted,

chunks.he: תֹּאמַר בִּטְרֵפָה שֶׁהָיְתָה לָהּ שְׁעַת הַכֹּשֶׁר.
chunks.en: should you say it about a treifah, which did have a time when it could be kosher?
chunks.st: does it necessarily follow that you should also say this in the case of a tereifa, which did have a period of potential fitness?
chunks.stMore: Perhaps, since the animal had a period of potential fitness its slaughter remains effective in preventing it from having the ritual impurity of a carcass.

chunks.en: Take back what you brought!
chunks.st: The mishna rejects this distinction: Take back to yourself this claim that you brought,
chunks.stMore: as it is insufficient.

chunks.he: הֲרֵי שֶׁנּוֹלְדָה טְרֵפָה מִן הַבֶּטֶן מִנַּיִן.
chunks.en: What about one born a treifah from the womb? How do we know?
chunks.st: What about a case where an animal was born as a tereifa from the womb, and so it never had a period of potential fitness? For such a case, from where is it derived that its slaughter renders it ritually pure?

chunks.en: No! If you said this about a non-kosher animal,
chunks.st: The mishna reformulates the distinction: No, if you say that slaughtering cannot prevent a prohibited animal from having the ritual impurity of a carcass with regard to a non-kosher animal,

chunks.en: whose kind never has shechitah,
chunks.st: which is distinct in that there are no animals of its kind that are permitted through slaughtering,
chunks.stMore: as the Torah states the concept of slaughtering only with regard to kosher animals,

chunks.en: should you say it about a treifah, whose kind does have shechitah?
chunks.st: does it necessarily follow that you should also say this with regard to a tereifa kosher animal, given that there are other animals of its kind that are permitted through slaughtering, i.e., kosher animals that are not tereifa?
chunks.stMore: Perhaps, since the concept of slaughtering is relevant to that kind of animal it can serve to prevent the animal from having the ritual impurity of a carcass even if the slaughter cannot render it permitted for consumption. The mishna notes: Based on this reasoning, one must conclude that with regard to

chunks.en: A baby animal born alive after eight months,
chunks.st: an eight-month-old fetus that was born alive,

chunks.en: its shechitah does not make it tahor,
chunks.st: slaughter does not render it ritually pure,

chunks.en: because its kind has no shechitah.
chunks.st: as there are no animals of its kind that are permitted through slaughtering.
chunks.stMore: The Torah applies the concept of slaughter only with regard to animals that were born full term.

mishnayos.summary: An unborn calf found inside a shechted animal may be eaten because of its mother's shechitah. If it is a full-term live calf, Rabbi Meir says it needs its own shechitah, but the Sages say its mother's shechitah is enough.

chunks.en: Someone who shechted an animal and found in it
chunks.st: In the case of one who slaughtered an animal and found within it an

chunks.en: an eight-month calf, alive or dead,
chunks.explain: Eight months is too early to be fully grown.
chunks.st: eight-month-old fetus, i.e., one that was not full term, whether it was alive or dead,

chunks.en: or a nine-month calf that is dead,
chunks.st: or a nine-month-old fetus, i.e., one that was full term, that was dead,
chunks.stMore: that fetus is permitted by virtue of the slaughter of its mother, as it is considered part of its mother. Therefore, its blood is considered part of its mother’s blood and is prohibited, so one must

chunks.en: he tears it open and takes out its blood.
chunks.st: tear the fetus and remove its blood before it may be consumed.

chunks.en: If he found a nine-month calf alive,
chunks.st: If he found within it a live nine-month-old fetus,

chunks.en: it needs shechitah,
chunks.st: it requires its own slaughter, as it is considered an independent full-fledged animal,

chunks.en: and he is liable for "it and its child".
chunks.explain: The Torah forbids shechting a mother and its child on the same day.
chunks.st: and if one slaughters both the mother and fetus on the same day, one is liable for violating the prohibition against slaughtering an animal itself and its offspring on the same day;

chunks.en: That is what Rabbi Meir says.
chunks.st: this is the statement of Rabbi Meir.

chunks.en: And the Sages say:
chunks.st: And the Rabbis say:
chunks.stMore: Even when the fetus is nine months old, it is still considered part of its mother, and

chunks.en: Its mother's shechitah makes it allowed.
chunks.st: the slaughter of its mother renders it permitted for consumption.

chunks.en: Rabbi Shimon Shezuri says:
chunks.st: Rabbi Shimon Shezuri says:

chunks.he: אֲפִלּוּ בֶן שְׁמֹנֶה שָׁנִים וְחוֹרֵשׁ בַּשָּׂדֶה,
chunks.en: Even if it grew up for years and is plowing in the field,
chunks.st: Even if the fetus emerged alive and is now five years old and plowing in the field,

chunks.en: its mother's shechitah made it allowed.
chunks.st: the earlier slaughter of its mother rendered it permitted and it does not require slaughter before it is eaten.

chunks.he: קְרָעָהּ וּמָצָא בָהּ בֶּן תִּשְׁעָה חַי,
chunks.en: If he tore the mother open and found in her a live nine-month calf,
chunks.st: But if one tore an animal, i.e., he killed it without slaughtering it, and inside he found a live nine-month-old fetus, everyone agrees that the fetus

chunks.en: it needs shechitah,
chunks.st: requires its own slaughter

chunks.en: because its mother was not shechted.
chunks.st: because its mother was not slaughtered.

mishnayos.summary: If an animal's legs were cut off below the knee joint it is kosher, but above it, it is a treifah. If a bone broke but most of the meat around it is whole, shechitah makes that leg allowed.

chunks.he: בְּהֵמָה שֶׁנֶּחְתְּכוּ רַגְלֶיהָ מִן הָאַרְכֻּבָּה וּלְמַטָּה,
chunks.en: An animal whose legs were cut off from the knee joint and down
chunks.st: With regard to an animal whose hind legs were severed, if they were severed from the leg joint and below, the animal is

chunks.en: is kosher. From the knee joint and up,
chunks.st: kosher; from the leg joint and above, the animal is thereby rendered a tereifa and is

chunks.en: it is pasul. And also one whose meeting of the sinews was taken out.
chunks.st: not kosher. And likewise, an animal whose convergence of sinews in the thigh was removed is a tereifa and is not kosher.

chunks.en: If the bone broke,
chunks.st: If the bone of a limb was broken but the limb was not completely severed, and the animal was then slaughtered,

chunks.en: if most of the meat around it is still whole,
chunks.st: if the majority of the flesh surrounding the bone is intact,

chunks.en: its shechitah makes it allowed.
chunks.st: the slaughter of the animal renders it permitted;

chunks.en: But if not,
chunks.st: but if not,

chunks.en: its shechitah does not make it allowed.
chunks.st: its slaughter does not render it permitted.

mishnayos.summary: The afterbirth found inside a shechted animal may be eaten by someone who does not mind, and it is not counted as food for tumah unless he plans to eat it. The mishnah also forbids burying or hanging it in superstitious ways.

chunks.he: הַשּׁוֹחֵט אֶת הַבְּהֵמָה וּמָצָא בָהּ שִׁלְיָא,
chunks.en: Someone who shechts an animal and finds the afterbirth inside it:
chunks.explain: The afterbirth is the sac that a baby animal grows in.

chunks.en: someone who is not disgusted may eat it.

words.note: Someone who is not picky or disgusted.

chunks.en: And it does not become tamei with the tumah
of food, nor with the tumah of a neveilah.
If he planned to eat it,
it can get the tumah of food, but
not the tumah of a neveilah.
An afterbirth that partly came out
may not be eaten.
It is a sign of a baby in a woman,
and a sign of a baby in an animal.
An animal having her first that lost an afterbirth:
he may throw it to the dogs.
But with korban animals, it must be buried.
But we may not bury it at a crossroads,
and we may not hang it on a tree,
because of the ways of the Emori.
chunks.explain: Superstitions of the non-Jews.

mishnayos.summary: The Torah forbids shechting a mother animal and its child on the same day ("oso v'es b'no"). This rule applies everywhere and always, for plain animals and for korbanos, and the mishnah shows what happens in different cases.

chunks.en: The rule of "it and its child"
chunks.explain: Not to shecht a mother animal and its child on the same day.
chunks.st: The prohibition against slaughtering an animal itself and its offspring

chunks.he: נוֹהֵג בֵּין בָּאָרֶץ בֵּין בְּחוּצָה לָאָרֶץ,
chunks.en: applies both in Eretz Yisrael and outside Eretz Yisrael,
chunks.st: applies both in Eretz Yisrael and outside of Eretz Yisrael, both

chunks.en: both when the Beis HaMikdash stands and when it does not,
chunks.st: in the presence, i.e., the time, of the Temple and not in the presence of the Temple, and it applies

chunks.en: with plain animals and with korbanos.
chunks.st: with regard to non-sacred animals and with regard to sacrificial animals.

chunks.he: כֵּיצַד. הַשּׁוֹחֵט אוֹתוֹ וְאֶת בְּנוֹ חֻלִּין בַּחוּץ,
chunks.en: How so? Someone who shechts it and its child, both plain animals, outside:
chunks.st: How so? In the case of one who slaughters an animal itself and its offspring,

chunks.en: both of them are kosher,
chunks.st: both of which are non-sacred, and slaughters them outside the Temple courtyard, both of the animals are fit for consumption,

chunks.en: and for the second one he gets the forty lashes.
chunks.explain: Malkus, the punishment for breaking certain Torah laws.
chunks.st: but for slaughtering the second animal, one incurs [sofeg] the forty lashes
chunks.stMore: for violating the prohibition: “You shall not slaughter it and its offspring both in one day” (Leviticus 22:28).

chunks.en: If they were korbanos, shechted outside the Beis HaMikdash:
chunks.st: If both animals were sacrificial animals slaughtered outside the Temple courtyard,

chunks.en: for the first one he deserves kares,
chunks.explain: Kares is a punishment from Heaven.
chunks.st: then for slaughtering the first animal, one is liable to receive excision from the World-to-Come [karet].
chunks.stMore: For slaughtering the second animal one is not liable to receive karet. The second animal was not fit for sacrifice, since one may not slaughter an animal and its offspring on the same day.

chunks.en: and both of them are pasul,
chunks.st: And both animals are disqualified for use as offerings,

chunks.en: and for both of them he gets the forty lashes.
chunks.st: and for the slaughter of both of them, one incurs forty lashes apiece:
chunks.stMore: The first being a sacrificial animal slaughtered outside the courtyard and the second being the offspring of an animal slaughtered that day.

chunks.en: Plain animals shechted inside:
chunks.st: If both animals were non-sacred and slaughtered inside the Temple courtyard,

chunks.en: both of them are pasul,
chunks.st: both of them are unfit to be sacrificed, being non-sacred animals slaughtered in the courtyard.

chunks.en: and for the second one he gets the forty lashes.
chunks.st: And for slaughter of the second animal, one incurs the forty lashes for slaughtering an animal and its offspring on a single day.

chunks.en: Korbanos shechted inside:
chunks.st: If both animals were sacrificial animals slaughtered inside the Temple courtyard,

chunks.en: the first one is kosher, and he is free of punishment,
chunks.st: the first is fit for sacrifice, and one who slaughters it is exempt from any punishment.

chunks.en: and for the second one he gets the forty lashes, and it is pasul.
chunks.st: But for slaughter of the second animal, one incurs the forty lashes for slaughtering an animal and its offspring on a single day, and it is unfit for sacrifice, because one was not allowed to slaughter it on that day.

mishnayos.summary: More cases of shechting a mother and its child on one day, when one is a plain animal and one a korban, or when one is shechted inside the Beis HaMikdash and one outside.

chunks.en: A plain animal, then a korban, outside:
chunks.st: If the first animal was non-sacred and the second a sacrificial animal, and both were slaughtered outside the Temple courtyard,

chunks.en: the first is kosher, and he is free of punishment,
chunks.st: the first is fit for consumption and one who slaughters it is exempt from any punishment.

chunks.en: and for the second he gets the forty lashes, and it is pasul.
chunks.st: But for slaughtering the second animal, one incurs the forty lashes for slaughtering an animal and its offspring on a single day, and the animal is unfit for sacrifice.

chunks.en: A korban, then a plain animal, outside:
chunks.st: If the first animal was a sacrificial animal and the second was non-sacred and both were slaughtered outside the Temple courtyard,

chunks.en: for the first he deserves kares, and it is pasul,
chunks.st: for the first animal, one is liable to receive karet for slaughtering a sacrificial animal outside the courtyard, and the animal is unfit for sacrifice.

chunks.en: and the second is kosher,

mishnayos.summary: The mitzvah of covering the blood (kisui hadam) after shechting a wild animal or a bird applies everywhere and always, but not for korbanos. For a koy, which may be a farm animal or a wild one, we cover the blood because of the doubt.

chunks.en: Covering the blood applies in Eretz Yisrael and outside Eretz Yisrael,
chunks.explain: After shechting a wild animal or bird, we cover its blood with earth.
chunks.st: The mitzva of covering the blood after slaughter is in effect both in Eretz Yisrael and outside of Eretz Yisrael, both

chunks.en: when the Beis HaMikdash stands and when it does not,
chunks.st: in the presence, i.e., the time, of the Temple and not in the presence of the Temple.

chunks.en: with plain animals, but not with korbanos.
chunks.st: And it is in effect with regard to non-sacred animals, but it is not in effect with regard to sacrificial ones.

chunks.en: Someone who makes cheese using the skin of a kosher stomach:
chunks.st: With regard to one who curdled milk by using the skin of the stomach of a kosher animal as a coagulant to make cheese, which may then have the taste of meat cooked in milk,

chunks.en: if it is enough to give a taste,
chunks.st: if the measure of the skin is enough to impart flavor to the milk,

chunks.en: it is forbidden.
chunks.st: that cheese is prohibited.

chunks.en: A kosher animal that nursed from a treifah:
chunks.st: In the case of a kosher animal that suckled milk from a tereifa, the milk in

chunks.en: the milk in its stomach is forbidden.
chunks.st: its stomach is prohibited, as the milk is from the tereifa.

chunks.en: A treifah that nursed from a kosher animal:
chunks.st: If it was a tereifa that suckled milk from a kosher animal, the milk in

chunks.en: the milk in its stomach is allowed,
chunks.st: its stomach is permitted,
chunks.stMore: as the milk is from the kosher animal. In both cases, the milk that an animal suckles has the status of the animal from which it was suckled, and not that of the animal which suckled,

chunks.en: because the milk is only gathered inside it.
chunks.st: because the milk is collected in its innards and is not an integral part of its body.

mishnayos.summary: Cheilev (forbidden fat) and blood are both forbidden. Cheilev is stricter in some ways, for korbanos, and blood is stricter because it applies to all animals and birds.

chunks.en: There is something stricter about cheilev than blood,
chunks.explain: Cheilev is certain fat that may not be eaten.
chunks.st: there are elements more stringent in the prohibition of fat than in that of blood,

chunks.en: and something stricter about blood than cheilev.
chunks.st: and likewise there are elements more stringent in the prohibition of blood than in that of fat.

chunks.en: Cheilev is stricter,
chunks.st: The elements more stringent in the prohibition of fat are the following: The first is

chunks.en: because with cheilev there is me'ilah,
chunks.explain: Me'ilah: using holy things for oneself.
chunks.st: that with regard to fat of an offering, one who derives benefit from it is liable for misuse of consecrated property.

chunks.he: וְחַיָּבִין עָלָיו מִשּׁוּם פִּגּוּל וְנוֹתָר וְטָמֵא,
chunks.en: and one is liable for it because of piggul, nosar, and being tamei,
chunks.explain: Piggul and nosar are korbanos that became forbidden to eat.
chunks.st: And second, one is liable for eating it due to violation of the prohibition of piggul, if it was from an offering that was slaughtered with the intent to sprinkle its blood or partake of it beyond its designated time, and due to the prohibition of notar, if it was from an offering whose period for consumption has expired. And third, if one is ritually impure, he is liable due to the prohibition of partaking of it while impure.

chunks.en: which is not so with blood.
chunks.st: This is not so with regard to blood,
chunks.stMore: as one is not liable in these cases for violating the prohibitions of piggul, notar, and partaking of offerings while impure, but rather is liable only for violating the prohibition of consuming blood.

chunks.en: And blood is stricter,
chunks.st: And the more stringent element in the prohibition of blood is

chunks.en: because blood applies to farm animals, wild animals and birds,
chunks.st: that the prohibition of blood applies to domesticated animals, undomesticated animals, and birds,

mishnayos.summary: Food must be the size of an egg to pass on the tumah of food. Things stuck to the meat, like skin, bones, and gravy, join with the meat to make that size, but not to make the kezayis of a neveilah.

chunks.en: The skin, and the gravy,
chunks.st: the attached hide, even if it is not fit for consumption, joins together with the meat to constitute an egg-bulk. And the same is true of the congealed gravy attached to the meat, although it is not eaten;

chunks.en: and the spices, and the leftover meat on the skin,
chunks.st: and likewise the spices added to flavor the meat, although they are not eaten; and the meat residue attached to the hide after flaying;

words.note: Bits of meat stuck to the skin.

chunks.en: and the bones, and the sinews,
chunks.st: and the bones; and the tendons;

chunks.en: and the horns, and the hooves,
chunks.st: and the lower section of the horns, which remains attached to the flesh when the rest of the horn is removed; and the upper section of the hooves, which remains attached to the flesh when the rest of the hoof is removed.

chunks.en: join together to make the tumah of food,
chunks.explain: Together with the meat, they make an egg's size.
chunks.st: All these items join together with the meat to constitute the requisite egg-bulk to impart the impurity of food.
chunks.stMore: Although if any of them was an egg-bulk they would not impart impurity of food, when attached to the meat they complete the measure.

chunks.en: but not the tumah of a neveilah.
chunks.st: But they do not join together to constitute the measure of an olive-bulk required to impart the impurity of animal carcasses.

chunks.en: Like this:
chunks.st: Similarly, there is another item that imparts impurity of food but not impurity of animal carcasses: In the case of

chunks.en: Someone who shechts a non-kosher animal for a non-Jew, and it is still twitching:
chunks.st: one who slaughters a non-kosher animal for a gentile and the animal is still twitching and comes into contact with a source of impurity, the animal becomes impure with impurity of food and

chunks.en: it makes things tamei with the tumah of food,
chunks.st: imparts impurity of food to other food,

chunks.en: but not with the tumah of a neveilah,
chunks.st: but does not impart impurity of animal carcasses

chunks.en: until it dies or until
chunks.st: until it dies, or

chunks.en: its head is cut off.
chunks.st: until one severs its head.

chunks.en: The Torah included more things for the tumah of food than
chunks.st: The mishna summarizes: The Torah included certain items to impart impurity of food

chunks.en: it included for the tumah of a neveilah.
chunks.st: beyond those which it included to impart impurity of animal carcasses.

chunks.en: Rabbi Yehudah says:
chunks.st: Rabbi Yehuda says: With regard to

chunks.en: Meat bits that were gathered together,
chunks.st: the meat residue attached to the hide after flaying that was collected,

chunks.he: אִם יֶשׁ בּוֹ כַזַּיִת בְּמָקוֹם אֶחָד,
chunks.en: if there is a kezayis of it in one place,
chunks.st: if there is an olive-bulk of it in one place it imparts impurity of an animal carcass, and one who contracts impurity from it and then eats consecrated foods or enters the Temple is

chunks.en: one is liable for it.
chunks.st: liable to receive karet.
chunks.stMore: By collecting it in one place, the person indicates that he considers it as meat.

mishnayos.stIntro: All foods that became ritually impure through contact with a source of impurity transmit impurity to other food and liquids only if the impure foods measure an egg-bulk. In that regard, the Sages ruled that even if a piece of meat itself is less than an egg-bulk,

mishnayos.summary: For some animals, the skin counts like the meat for tumah, like a pig's skin and the soft skin of young animals. Once they are tanned, they are tahor, except for a person's skin.

chunks.en: These are the ones whose skin counts like their meat:
The skin of a person,
and the skin of a pig raised among people.
Rabbi Yosei says:
Even the skin of a wild pig.
And the skin of a young camel's hump,
and the skin of a young calf's head,
and the skin of the hooves,
and the skin of a private place,
and the skin of an unborn calf,
and the skin under the tail,
and the skin of the anakah, the ko'ach, the leta'ah, and the chomet.
chunks.explain: Four kinds of small creeping animals, like lizards.

chunks.en: Rabbi Yehudah says:
The leta'ah is like the weasel.
chunks.explain: Its skin does not count like its meat.

chunks.en: And all of them, if he tanned them, or walked
on them long enough to tan them,
are tahor, except for the skin of a person.
Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri says:
The eight sheratzim have skins.
chunks.explain: Sheratzim are small creeping animals that make things tamei.

mishnayos.summary: While an animal is being skinned, the skin still counts as connected to the meat for tumah until enough of it is taken off, depending on what he is making from the skin.

chunks.en: Someone who skins a farm animal or a wild animal,
chunks.st: Nevertheless, in the case of one who flays either a domesticated animal or an undomesticated animal;

chunks.en: a tahor one or a tamei one,
chunks.st: a ritually pure animal that was slaughtered properly and afterward came in contact with impurity, e.g., the one flaying it is impure, or a ritually impure unslaughtered carcass;

chunks.en: a small one or a big one:
chunks.st: a small animal, e.g., sheep, or a large animal, e.g., cattle;
chunks.stMore: and even after flaying the animal’s hide is still partially attached to the flesh, the hide’s halakhic status remains that of flesh in some circumstances.

chunks.en: for a rug, until he skins a handful.
chunks.st: These circumstances are: If he is flaying the animal for the purpose of using the hide as a carpet, a tablecloth, or to drape over a couch, in which case he would cut the hide along the length of the animal from head to tail and then remove the hide from both sides, its halakhic status remains that of flesh until he has flayed the measure of grasping the hide, i.e., two handbreadths.

chunks.en: For a leather jug, until he skins the chest.
chunks.st: And if he is flaying the animal for the purpose of crafting a leather jug, in which case he cuts a circle near the animal’s neck and removes the hide in a downward movement, its halakhic status remains that of flesh until he flays the animal’s entire breast.

chunks.en: If he skins it starting from the legs, all of it is connected for tumah,
chunks.st: In the case of one who seeks to fashion a jug and begins flaying from the legs, until he removes the animal’s hide in its entirety, the entire hide is considered as having a connection with the flesh and its halakhic status remains that of flesh with regard to impurity, i.e., with regard

words.en: one who starts from the legs

chunks.en: to become tamei and to make tamei.
chunks.st: to becoming impure and with regard to imparting impurity. If one removed the entire hide except for

chunks.en: The skin on the neck:
chunks.st: the hide over the neck,

chunks.en: Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri says:
chunks.st: Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri says:

chunks.en: It is not connected.
chunks.st: It is not considered to have a connection to the flesh,

chunks.en: And the Sages say:
chunks.st: and the Rabbis say: It is considered to have a

chunks.en: It is connected until he skins all of it.
chunks.st: connection to the flesh until he removes the animal’s hide in its entirety, including the neck.

mishnayos.stIntro: The halakhic status of the hide of an animal after it was flayed is no longer like its flesh in terms of becoming impure and imparting impurity.

mishnayos.summary: If a neveilah's skin has a kezayis of meat on it, touching a strand or hair of it makes a person tamei. Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva argue about two half-kezaysim of meat on the skin.

chunks.en: A skin that has a kezayis of meat on it:
chunks.st: In the case of a hide of an unslaughtered carcass upon which there is an olive-bulk of flesh,

chunks.en: someone who touches a strand of meat coming out of it,
chunks.st: one who touches a strand of flesh emerging from the flesh

chunks.en: or a hair on the other side of it,
chunks.st: or a hair that is on the side of the hide opposite the flesh

chunks.en: is tamei.
chunks.st: is ritually impure.
chunks.stMore: Although he did not touch an olive-bulk of the flesh, he is rendered impure with the impurity of an unslaughtered carcass. The reason is that the strand of flesh has the same status as the flesh itself, and the hair is considered protection to the flesh, which also has the same status as the flesh with regard to one who touches it.

chunks.en: If there were two half-kezaysim on it,
chunks.st: If upon the hide there were two half olive-bulks, the hide

chunks.en: it makes tamei by carrying, but not by touching.
chunks.st: imparts the impurity of an unslaughtered carcass by means of carrying, because one moves them together, but not by means of contact with the flesh, because one touches them separately;

chunks.en: That is what Rabbi Yishmael says.
chunks.st: this is the statement of Rabbi Yishmael.

chunks.en: Rabbi Akiva says:
chunks.st: Rabbi Akiva says: The hide does not impart impurity,

chunks.en: Not by touching and not by carrying.
chunks.st: neither by means of contact nor by means of carrying.

chunks.en: And Rabbi Akiva agrees about two half-kezaysim
chunks.st: And Rabbi Akiva concedes in the case of

chunks.en: that he stuck on a stick and moved,
chunks.st: two half olive-bulks where one skewered them with a wood chip and moved them

chunks.en: that he is tamei.
chunks.st: that he is impure.

chunks.he: וּמִפְּנֵי מָה רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא מְטַהֵר בָּעוֹר,
chunks.en: So why does Rabbi Akiva say he is tahor with the skin?
chunks.st: And for what reason does Rabbi Akiva deem one ritually pure in a case where he moved both half olive-bulks with the hide, as in that case, too, he moved them together?

chunks.en: Because the skin cancels them.
chunks.explain: The skin keeps the two halves apart.
chunks.st: It is because the hide separates between them and nullifies them.

mishnayos.summary: A thigh bone of a dead person or of a korban makes tamei even when closed. A thigh bone of a neveilah or a sheretz makes tamei only if it has a hole, because the marrow inside is what makes tamei.

chunks.en: The thigh bone of a dead person, or the thigh bone of a korban,
chunks.st: With regard to the thigh bone of a human corpse, and the thigh bone of a sacrificial animal
chunks.stMore: that was rendered unfit as piggul, i.e., an offering that was sacrificed with the intent to consume it after its designated time, or notar, i.e., part of an offering left over after the time allotted for its consumption,

chunks.he: הַנּוֹגֵעַ בָּהֶן, בֵּין סְתוּמִים בֵּין נְקוּבִים, טָמֵא.
chunks.en: someone who touches them, whether they are closed or have a hole, is tamei.
chunks.st: whether these thigh bones were sealed and there was no access to the marrow, or whether they were perforated and there was access to the marrow, one who touches them is ritually impure.
chunks.stMore: The reason is that a piece of bone of a corpse the size of a barley grain imparts impurity, and the bone of a sacrificial animal that was disqualified in this manner imparts impurity by rabbinic decree via contact.

chunks.en: The thigh bone of a neveilah or the thigh bone of a sheretz:
chunks.st: With regard to the thigh bone of an unslaughtered carcass and the thigh bone of a creeping animal,

chunks.en: someone who touches them when they are closed
chunks.st: one who touches them when they are sealed remains

chunks.en: stays tahor. If it has any hole at all,
chunks.st: ritually pure. If one of these thigh bones was perforated at all,

chunks.en: it makes tamei by touching.
chunks.st: it imparts impurity via contact,
chunks.stMore: as in that case contact with the bone is tantamount to contact with the marrow.

chunks.en: How do we know that also by carrying?
chunks.st: From where is it derived that even with regard to impurity transmitted via carrying there is a distinction between sealed and perforated thigh bones?

chunks.en: The pasuk says (Vayikra 11):
chunks.st: It is derived from a verse, as the verse states: “

chunks.en: "the one who touches" and "the one who carries."
chunks.st: One who touches the carcass thereof shall be impure until the evening; and one who carries the carcass thereof shall be impure until the evening” (Leviticus 11:39–40), indicating:

chunks.en: What comes under the rule of touching
chunks.st: That which enters the category of impurity via contact,

chunks.en: comes under the rule of carrying.
chunks.st: enters the category of impurity via carrying;

chunks.en: What does not come under the rule of touching
chunks.st: that which does not enter the category of impurity via contact,

chunks.en: does not come under the rule of carrying.
chunks.st: does not enter the category of impurity via carrying.

mishnayos.summary: A sheretz's egg with a chick growing inside is tahor while closed, but tamei once it has a hole. The mishnah also talks about a mouse that is half flesh and half earth.

chunks.en: An egg of a sheretz with a baby forming inside
chunks.st: The egg of a creeping animal in which tissue of an embryo developed and one who comes into contact with the egg are

chunks.en: is tahor. If it got any hole at all,
chunks.st: ritually pure, as the impure creeping animal is hermetically sealed. But if one perforated the egg with a hole of any size, one who comes in contact with the egg is

chunks.he: טְמֵאָה. עַכְבָּר שֶׁחֶצְיוֹ בָשָׂר וְחֶצְיוֹ אֲדָמָה,
chunks.en: it is tamei. A mouse that is half flesh and half earth:
chunks.explain: People thought some mice grew out of the ground.
chunks.st: ritually impure. In the case of a mouse that grows from the ground and is half-flesh half-earth,

chunks.en: someone who touches the flesh
chunks.st: one who touches the half that is flesh is

chunks.en: is tamei. If he touches the earth,
chunks.st: impure; one who touches the half that is earth is

chunks.en: he is tahor. Rabbi Yehudah says:
chunks.st: pure. Rabbi Yehuda says:

chunks.he: אַף הַנּוֹגֵעַ בָּאֲדָמָה שֶׁכְּנֶגֶד הַבָּשָׂר, טָמֵא:
chunks.en: Even someone who touches the earth next to the flesh is tamei.
chunks.st: Even one who touches the half that is earth where it is adjacent to the flesh is ritually impure.

mishnayos.summary: A limb or meat that is partly cut and hanging from an animal can get the tumah of food once it is made wet. Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon argue about what happens when the animal is shechted or dies.

chunks.en: A limb or meat hanging loose from an animal
chunks.st: The limb of an animal, with flesh, sinews, and bones, and the flesh of an animal, that were partially severed and remain hanging from the animal
chunks.stMore: do not have the halakhic status of a limb severed from a living animal, which imparts impurity like an unslaughtered carcass, or of flesh severed from a living animal, which is ritually pure, respectively. If one had intent to eat the limb or the flesh, the limb or flesh becomes impure if it comes in contact with a source of impurity, and they

chunks.en: make things tamei with the tumah of food while still in their place,
chunks.st: impart impurity as food to other foods and liquids, although they remain in their place attached to the animal.

chunks.en: and they need to be made ready.
chunks.explain: Made wet by certain liquids, so they can become tamei.
chunks.st: But in order for them to become impure, they need to be rendered susceptible to impurity through contact with one of the seven liquids that facilitate susceptibility. If

chunks.en: If the animal was shechted,
chunks.st: the animal was slaughtered,
chunks.stMore: although this act of slaughter does not render it permitted for consumption by a Jew (see 73b), the limb and the flesh

chunks.en: they were made ready by its blood.
chunks.st: were thereby rendered susceptible to impurity by coming in contact with the blood of the slaughtered animal, as blood is one of the seven liquids;

chunks.en: That is what Rabbi Meir says.
chunks.st: this is the statement of Rabbi Meir.

chunks.en: Rabbi Shimon says:
chunks.st: Rabbi Shimon says:

chunks.en: They were not made ready.
chunks.st: They were not rendered susceptible to impurity through the animal’s own blood;
chunks.stMore: they are rendered susceptible only once they have been wet with another liquid. If

chunks.en: If the animal died,
chunks.st: the animal died without slaughter,

chunks.en: the meat needs to be made ready.
chunks.st: the hanging flesh needs to be rendered susceptible to impurity in order to become impure,
chunks.stMore: as its halakhic status is that of flesh severed from a living animal, which is ritually pure and does not have the status of an unslaughtered carcass.

chunks.he: הָאֵבָר מְטַמֵּא מִשּׁוּם אֵבָר מִן הַחַי
chunks.en: The limb makes tamei as a limb from a living animal,
chunks.st: The hanging limb imparts impurity as a limb severed from a living animal

chunks.en: but it does not make tamei as a limb of a neveilah.
chunks.st: but does not impart impurity as the limb of an unslaughtered carcass;

chunks.en: That is what Rabbi Meir says.
chunks.st: this is the statement of Rabbi Meir.

chunks.en: And Rabbi Shimon says it is tahor.
chunks.st: And Rabbi Shimon deems the limb ritually pure.

mishnayos.summary: A limb or flesh hanging loose from a living person is tahor. Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon argue about the limb after the person dies.

chunks.en: A limb or flesh hanging loose from a person
chunks.st: The limb and the flesh of a person that were partially severed and remain hanging from a person

chunks.en: are tahor. If the person died,
chunks.st: are ritually pure, although there is no potential for healing. If the person died,

chunks.en: the flesh is tahor.
chunks.st: the hanging flesh is ritually pure, as its halakhic status is that of flesh severed from a living person.

chunks.he: הָאֵבָר מְטַמֵּא מִשּׁוּם אֵבָר מִן הַחַי
chunks.en: The limb makes tamei as a limb from the living,
chunks.st: The hanging limb imparts impurity as a limb severed from the living

chunks.he: וְאֵינוֹ מְטַמֵּא מִשּׁוּם אֵבָר מִן הַמֵּת,
chunks.en: but it does not make tamei as a limb from the dead.
chunks.st: and does not impart impurity as a limb from a corpse;

chunks.en: That is what Rabbi Meir says.
chunks.st: this is the statement of Rabbi Meir.

chunks.en: And Rabbi Shimon says it is tahor.
chunks.st: And Rabbi Shimon deems the flesh and the limb ritually pure.

mishnayos.summary: When a plain animal is shechted, the foreleg, the cheeks and the stomach are given to the Kohen (the matanos). This applies everywhere and always, but not to korbanos, as the pasuk teaches.

chunks.en: The foreleg, the cheeks, and the stomach apply
chunks.explain: These parts of a shechted animal are gifts for the Kohen.
chunks.st: The mitzva to give the foreleg, the jaw, and the maw of slaughtered animals to the priests, known as the gifts of the priesthood, applies both

chunks.en: in Eretz Yisrael and outside Eretz Yisrael,
chunks.st: in Eretz Yisrael and outside of Eretz Yisrael,

chunks.en: when the Beis HaMikdash stands and when it does not,
chunks.st: in the presence of the Temple and not in the presence of the Temple, and it applies

chunks.en: with plain animals but not with korbanos.
chunks.st: to non-sacred animals, but not to sacrificial animals.

chunks.en: Because one might have reasoned:
chunks.st: It is necessary to emphasize that it does not apply to sacrificial animals, as by right it should be inferred a fortiori:

chunks.en: If plain animals,
chunks.st: If non-sacred animals,

chunks.en: which do not have to give the chest and the thigh,
chunks.st: which are not obligated to have the breast and thigh taken from them and given to the priest,

chunks.en: must give the matanos,
chunks.st: are obligated to have gifts of the priesthood given from them,

chunks.en: then korbanos, which do give the chest and the thigh,
chunks.st: then with regard to sacrificial animals, which are obligated to have the breast and thigh given from them,

chunks.en: shouldn't they surely have to give the matanos?
chunks.st: is it not right that they should be obligated to have gifts of the priesthood given from them?

chunks.en: So the pasuk says (Vayikra 7):
chunks.st: Therefore, the verse states: “For the breast of waving and the thigh of giving I have taken of the children of Israel from the sacrifice of the peace offerings,

chunks.en: "And I gave them to Aharon the Kohen
chunks.st: and have given them to Aaron the priest

chunks.en: and to his sons, as a rule forever."
chunks.st: and to his sons as a due forever from the children of Israel” (Leviticus 7:34), from which it is derived that the priest

chunks.he: אֵין לוֹ אֶלָּא מַה שֶּׁאָמוּר בָּעִנְיָן:
chunks.en: He gets only what is said in that section.
chunks.st: has only that which is stated with regard to that matter, i.e., the breast and the thigh, and not the foreleg, the jaw and the maw.

mishnayos.summary: An animal that had a lasting blemish before it was made holy, once redeemed, is almost like a plain animal. But if it became holy first and got a blemish later, much of its holiness stays even after it is redeemed.

chunks.en: All korbanos that had a lasting blemish
chunks.explain: A blemish (mum) makes an animal unfit to be a korban.
chunks.st: All sacrificial animals in

chunks.en: before they were made holy, and they were redeemed,
chunks.st: which a permanent blemish preceded their consecration do not assume inherent sanctity, and only their value is consecrated.

chunks.en: must give the bechor and the matanos,
chunks.st: And once they were redeemed, they are obligated in the mitzva of a firstborn, i.e., their offspring are subject to being counted a firstborn, and in the gifts of the priesthood,

chunks.en: and they become plain,
chunks.st: and they can emerge from their sacred status and assume non-sacred status

chunks.en: to be sheared and to be worked.
chunks.st: with regard to being shorn and with regard to being utilized for labor,
chunks.stMore: as it is prohibited to shear animals with sacred status or utilize them for labor.

chunks.en: Their babies and their milk are allowed after they were redeemed.

mishnayos.summary: We may not take the mother bird with her children, even for the mitzvah of making a metzora tahor. If the Torah promises long life for this easy mitzvah, surely there is a great reward for harder mitzvos.

chunks.he: לֹא יִטֹּל אָדָם אֵם עַל הַבָּנִים,
chunks.en: A person may not take the mother with the children,
chunks.st: A person may not take the mother bird with the offspring

chunks.en: even to make a metzora tahor.
chunks.explain: A metzora is a person with tzaraas; birds are used to make him tahor.
chunks.st: even if he takes the mother for use as part of the ritual to purify the leper.
chunks.stMore: The mishna compares the reward for performing the mitzva of sending away the mother bird from the nest to the reward for performing other mitzvot:

chunks.he: וּמָה אִם מִצְוָה קַלָּה שֶׁהִיא כְאִסָּר,
chunks.en: If for an easy mitzvah that costs only an issar,
chunks.explain: An issar is a small coin.
chunks.st: And if with regard to the sending away of the mother bird, which is a mitzva whose performance is simple, as it entails a loss of no more than an issar, i.e., the value of the mother bird,

chunks.en: the Torah says (Devarim 22):
chunks.st: the Torah says: “

chunks.en: "So that it will be good for you, and you will live long,"
chunks.st: That it may be well with you, and that you may prolong your days” (Deuteronomy 22:7),

chunks.he: קַל וָחֹמֶר עַל מִצְוֹת חֲמוּרוֹת שֶׁבַּתּוֹרָה:
chunks.en: then surely the same is true for the harder mitzvos in the Torah!
chunks.st: it may be derived by a fortiori inference that the reward is no less for the fulfillment of the mitzvot in the Torah whose performance is demanding.

words.note: A kal vachomer: how much more so.
